Functional annotation & region-level analysis

  • Show All Code

Annotation and Interpretation

At this point the EWAS is done: we have a per-CpG table of effect sizes and p-values, BACON-adjusted for residual inflation (notebook 06), and — if we chose the stratified route — a METAL meta-analysis of the strata (notebook 07). Next we introduce functional annotation and region-level analysis. Previously it was mentioned that the snakemake pipeline can do differentially methylated region analysis in addition to the EWAS. But, it wasn’t really explained what that is or why you would want to do it. Here we more fully detail functional annotation and secondary analysis (including regional analyses) that are a necessary part in interpretation of results.

  1. CpG-level functional annotation — attach genomic coordinates, gene context, CpG-island relationship, and expression links to every probe, so the top hits can be read as “this CpG sits in the promoter of gene X” rather than “cg16340178”.
  2. Region-level analysis (DMRs) — ask whether spatially clustered CpGs move together. A differentially methylated region (DMR) can be highly significant even when no single CpG in it survives genome-wide correction, because neighboring probes are correlated and that correlation carries signal (Pedersen et al. 2012; Peters et al. 2015).

For functional annotation of the EWAS results we use Wanding Zhou’s hg38 EPIC annotation resources (Zhou et al. 2017). Zhou recently (July of 2026) made a major update of his website and released new versions of his resources (v8.1). This tutorial implements some of the newest version of Zhou’s files in addition to some ‘legacy’ files. The Snakemake pipeline uses entirely legacy files at the moment, but will be updated to use the latest versions in the next release. Most of the annotation in this chapter is hg38, but not all of it. The enrichment tools goregion, gometh and methylGSA default to Illumina’s hg19 annotation package; here we pass each of them Zhou’s hg38 annotation instead, but the knowYourCG knowledgebases and the web tools still rest partly or wholly on hg19. The table below lists the build and source behind each section. It matters most where the chapter compares tools, because two tools built on different annotations are not a like-for-like comparison. For tools that take probe IDs rather than coordinates, the build shows up in which genes or features each probe was assigned to, not in any coordinate you see.

Section Tool Genome build Annotation source
Part 1: gene and CpG-island context Zhou manifests hg38 Zhou, GENCODE v41 and v36
Part 1: eQTM layer BIOS cis-eQTM catalog hg19 (original mapping; joined by probe ID) BIOS consortium, gene symbols re-mapped to current HGNC
Part 2: region calling comb-p, ENmix::combp hg38 Zhou coordinates
Part 2: annotating the DMR overlap with UCSC tables hg38 UCSC refGene, cpgIslandExt, HGNC
Part 2: region enrichment missMethyl::goregion hg38 Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with anno =)
Part 3: gene-set enrichment missMethyl::gometh hg38 Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with anno =)
Part 3: gene-set enrichment methylGSA hg38 Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with FullAnnot =)
Part 3: regulatory-feature enrichment knowYourCG hg38, except chromatin states (hg19) Zhou knowledgebases (Cistrome, Roadmap)
Part 3: web tools EWAS Toolkit, eFORGE hg19 Illumina; Roadmap/ENCODE

The three tables used for annotation, all downloadable from the zhou-lab GitHub are:

  • EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz — gene model: gene names, transcript biotypes, and signed distance to the nearest TSS.
  • EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v36.tsv.gz — the v36 table additionally carries the CpG-island (CGI) relation column we use for island context.
  • EPIC.hg38.coord.tsv.gz — remapped hg38 coordinates. Note this table is keyed by genomic position and carries no probeID column, so it cannot be merged onto results by probe; the v41 manifest above already supplies CpG_chrm/CpG_beg/CpG_end and is what we actually join.

Methylation is often a mediator of change. The environment can cause changes to methylation, which subsequently causes change in gene expression. Methylation sites that cause changes in gene expression are called expression quantitative trait methylation sites (eQTMs). So, one additional external layer, the BIOS cis-eQTM catalog (whole-blood methylation→expression links) was added to expand the functional annotation. This helps identify which (if any) effector gene may be behind methylation change. I recommend reading more into the BIOS eQTM catalog more before using and reporting the results as there are some distinct limitations (only 450k methylation array probes were tested, European-ancestry only cohort, original analysis uses hg19 mapping). This part of the functional annotation was added to the EWAS Snakemake upon request from a reviewer for the information.

NoteThis notebook and the Snakemake pipeline

The krferrier/EWAS pipeline automates part of this chapter — its annotate.smk and dmr.smk rules run the same annotation join and the same comb-p region detection we walk through manually. It does not yet run pathway enrichment (Part 3); that is planned for the next update. We reproduce the steps by hand so the logic is clearly layed out.

Code 
library(data.table)      # fread()/fwrite() and the := joins used all through this chapter
library(ggplot2)         # the two context bar charts in Part 1

Part 1 — CpG-level functional annotation

What annotation resources exist, and which to trust

An EPIC probe ID like cg16340178 is the Illumina name for a CpG. To interpret it we need to know where it lands in the genome and what functional element it tags. Historically people reached for the hg19 Illumina/minfi manifest for this, but its coordinates are a genome build behind current references and its gene mapping is generous (it lists any transcript overlapping the probe). Zhou’s resources supersede it:

Zhou hg38 table What it gives Column(s) we use
manifest.gencode.v41 gencode v41 gene model genesUniq, transcriptTypes, distToTSS
manifest.gencode.v36 earlier gene model that also carries CGI relation CGIposition (Island / N_/S_Shore / N_/S_Shelf / open sea)
coord remapped hg38 coordinates CpG_chrm, CpG_beg, CpG_end
BIOS cis-eQTM (Bonder et al. 2017) (external) genes whose expression tracks the CpG’s methylation in whole blood likely downstream effector gene

The annotation join

We start from the BACON-adjusted top-table saved in chapter 06 and left-join the Zhou tables on probe ID. The v41 gene table can list several TSS distances per probe (one per transcript); we keep the nearest, which is what defines the promoter call below.

NoteWhat this section needs

This section starts from data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz, written by chapter 06. If you did not run that chapter, fetch the published checkpoint instead:

Terminal
./get_data.sh F_ewas_results
Code 
# The two Zhou gencode manifests are read straight from the zhou-lab repository.
zhou_epic <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotationData/",
                    "6d176d6e7e56465403d4478a09fe11b983eeb721/Anno/EPIC/")

# 1. EWAS results: the BACON-adjusted toptable from chapter 06
tt <- fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")

# 2. Zhou gencode v41 gene model: gene names, biotypes, signed distance to TSS
v41 <- fread(paste0(zhou_epic, "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz"))
# a probe with several transcripts has several distToTSS values (';'-joined);
# keep the one nearest the TSS — this is what the promoter definition uses
nearest_tss <- function(x) {
  v <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(strsplit(x, ";")[[1]]))
  if (all(is.na(v))) return(NA_real_)
  v[which.min(abs(v))]
}
# one function call per probe over the whole manifest: the slow line here
v41[, distTSS := vapply(distToTSS, nearest_tss, numeric(1))]

# 3. CpG-island relation — only the v36 gene table carries CGIposition
v36 <- fread(paste0(zhou_epic, "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v36.tsv.gz"),
             select = c("probeID","CGIposition"))
v36[, island := fifelse(is.na(CGIposition) | CGIposition == "", "OpenSea", CGIposition)]

# 4. Join everything on probe ID.
#    all.x = TRUE: every tested CpG stays in the table, annotated or not.
annotated <- tt |>
  merge(v41[, .(probe = probeID, CpG_chrm, CpG_beg, CpG_end,
                genesUniq, transcriptTypes, distTSS)], by = "probe", all.x = TRUE) |>
  merge(v36[, .(probe = probeID, island)], by = "probe", all.x = TRUE)

# 5. Zhou's gene-feature convention: the gene model runs from 1.5 kb upstream of
#    the TSS through the termination site. A probe within +/-1.5 kb of a TSS is
#    promoter-associated; genic but beyond that is gene body; no gene is intergenic.
annotated[, feature := fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq %in% c("", "NA"), "Intergenic",
                        fifelse(!is.na(distTSS) & abs(distTSS) <= 1500, "Promoter", "Gene body"))]
# rank by the BACON p-value
setorder(annotated, bacon.p)

# The deposited table is written a few sections down, after the eQTM columns are
# joined on, so that the file on disk carries every annotation this chapter builds.

On our Grady PTSD subset this annotates all 756,251 CpGs with hg38 coordinates and maps 647,034 (85.6%) to at least one gencode v41 gene. The remaining ~14% are intergenic. This is expected since a large fraction of the EPIC array deliberately targets enhancers and open sea away from genes.

The annotated top hits

Code 
t10 <- head(annotated, 10)[, .(
  probe, chr = CpG_chrm, pos = CpG_beg,
  # an intergenic probe has no symbol; print a dash rather than NA
  gene = fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq == "", "-", genesUniq),
  distTSS = round(distTSS), feature, island,
  # delta_beta is chapter 06's case−control β difference; ×100 puts it in
  # percentage points, which is how the prose discusses effect sizes
  delta_beta = round(100 * delta_beta, 2),
  bacon_p = signif(bacon.p, 3), bacon_FDR = signif(bacon.adj.P, 3))]
setnames(t10, c("probe","chr","pos","gene","distToTSS","feature","island",
                "\u0394\u03b2 (pp)","BACON p","BACON FDR"))
fwrite(t10, "data/08_annotation/top10_display.csv")

Now the list has biological context. The top-ranked CpG cg15434749 is intergenic open sea on chr8 with no nearby gencode v41 gene. cg25717994 sits essentially on the EDNRB TSS (distToTSS = −12 bp, so promoter by Zhou’s ±1.5 kb rule); cg18321729 tags the PKM promoter (−168 bp); cg26747885 is in a CpG island (Island) at the SOCS3 TSS (distToTSS = 455 bp). Four of the top ten fall within 1.5 kb of a TSS. The trend of top-ranked CpGs being in a promotor region is not seen in this analysis, but may appear in a full scale, well-powered EWAS. No CpG clears the Bonferroni significance threshold (the top CpG has BACON p ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ against a threshold of ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻⁸), and none passes FDR < 0.05 (lowest BACON FDR 0.090). Read this table as ‘nominally significant’ rather than ‘statistically significant’.

In a real study this table is the hand-off point to the enrichment tools in Part 3 and to comparison against published EWAS catalogs.

Where the top hits sit relative to genes and islands

A useful sanity check is to compare the distribution of the top-ranked CpGs across gene features and island context against the array background. A well-powered signal often enriches in promoters and island shores.

Code 
# The two figures below, and the percentages their captions quote. Needs
# `annotated` from the join above; the PNGs it writes are the ones included
# underneath.
TOPN <- 1000
top  <- head(annotated, TOPN)          # `annotated` is already ordered by bacon.p

# One helper for both panels: tabulate a column in the top set and in the whole
# tested set, then convert to a percentage *within* each set, because the two
# sets differ in size by three orders of magnitude and raw counts would not be
# comparable.
mk <- function(col, lev) {
  a <- data.table(set = "Top 1,000",  grp = factor(top[[col]], levels = lev))
  b <- data.table(set = "All tested", grp = factor(annotated[[col]], levels = lev))
  d <- rbind(a, b)[!is.na(grp), .N, by = .(set, grp)]
  d[, pct := 100 * N / sum(N), by = set]
  # top set first, so the series the reader is asking about leads the legend
  d[, set := factor(set, levels = c("Top 1,000", "All tested"))]
  d
}
fd <- mk("feature", c("Promoter", "Gene body", "Intergenic"))
# island levels in genomic order: island, its two shores, its two shelves, then
# everything else — alphabetical order would scramble that
id <- mk("island", c("Island","N_Shore","S_Shore","N_Shelf","S_Shelf","OpenSea"))

ctx_plot <- function(d, xlab) {
  ggplot(d, aes(grp, pct, fill = set)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Top 1,000`  = "#1A6B75",   # teal
                                 `All tested` = "#B8873F"),  # sand
                      name = NULL) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "% of CpGs")
}
ggsave("data/08_annotation/08_feature_distribution.png",
       plot = ctx_plot(fd, "gene feature (Zhou gencode v41)"),
       width = 7, height = 3.2, dpi = 300)
ggsave("data/08_annotation/08_island_distribution.png",
       plot = ctx_plot(id, "CpG-island relation (Zhou CGI)"),
       width = 7, height = 3.2, dpi = 300)

The distributions move only modestly between the top 1,000 and the background (Figure 1, Figure 2). The top-set leans slightly toward islands but not toward promoters, and it’s not clear if that pattern is more than chance. The bar chart above is a useful visual indicator, but not a formal enrichment test, which is covered in Part 3 of this chapter.

The BIOS eQTM layer: methylation that tracks expression

Annotated methylation data often includes a column with the ‘nearest gene’ to the CpG. This is a useful annotation for identifying where in the genome the CpG is physically located and can hint at potential functional impact. For example, evidence of methylation at CpG in a promotor region of a gene could indicate a cis-effect between the CpG and expression of that gene. However, in reality, DNA sequence is not linear, it has 3-dimensional structure. In 3D space, the ‘nearest gene’ in terms of base-pairs may not be the gene that the methylation site is having an effect on. The answer we really want is is whether a CpG actually affects gene expression. The BIOS consortium answered this directly by pairing whole-blood methylation with RNA-seq in ~3,000 samples and testing every cis CpG–transcript pair, producing a catalog of cis-eQTMs (Bonder et al. 2017). This information provides the likely effector gene behind a methylation change — which is not necessarily the nearest gene.

NoteBIOS consortium meQTL catalogs

The BIOS consortium also provides catalogs for cis- and trans-meQTLs (methylation Quantitative Trait Loci), which provide evidence of genetic loci that cause changes to methylation status. This annotation information was not incorporated into the snakemake pipeline and how to merge it in will not be covered in this tutorial as it would require lifting over that data from hg19 to hg38 and only represents meQTLs for CpGs from the 450k array. If you have both methylation and genetic data for your sample, which is often the case, you can perform cis- and trans-meQTL testing yourself. The eQTM relationships require having gene expression and methylation data, which is less common and why the effort was made to liftover and update the eQTM data from the BIOS consortium.

The catalogs are keyed on Ensembl gene IDs; the pipeline’s prepare_bios_eqtm_annotation.R helper re-maps those to current HGNC symbols for eQTM data.

NoteWhat this section needs

This section reads data/08_annotation/bios_eqtm_hgnc_annotated.tsv.gz, which is committed to the repository, so there is nothing to fetch. It is the output of a script from the EWAS snakemake pipeline, prepare_bios_eqtm_annotation.R. Please refer to the source code in the EWAS repo if you’d like to rebuild this file yourself.

Code 
# Extends `annotated` from the join above. The two files it writes at the end
# are the ones every later section of this chapter reads.

eqtm <- fread("data/08_annotation/bios_eqtm_hgnc_annotated.tsv.gz")

# collapse to one row per CpG: effector gene(s) + strongest eQTM FDR
eq <- eqtm[HGNCName_GRCh38 != "" & !is.na(HGNCName_GRCh38),
           .(BIOS_eQTM_genes  = paste(sort(unique(HGNCName_GRCh38)), collapse = ";"),
             BIOS_eQTM_minFDR = min(as.numeric(FDR), na.rm = TRUE)),
           by = .(probe = SNPName)]

annotated <- merge(annotated, eq, by = "probe", all.x = TRUE)
setorder(annotated, bacon.p)      # merge() re-sorts by the join key; rank it again

# --- what Part 1 hands on -------------------------------------------------
# Export the annotation data as a .csv (as is found in the Zenodo tier H_annotation) and an RDS.
fwrite(annotated, "data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_zhou.csv.gz")
saveRDS(annotated, "data/08_annotation/annotated.rds")

On our subset the eQTM layer annotates 10,803 of the 756,251 tested CpGs (1.4%) with at least one expression-linked effector gene. I will reiterate, there are so few annotations because the BIOS eQTM catalog was curated using the 450k methylation array, and not all probes used in the 450k array were included in the 850k array. In addition, the BIOS catalog only keeps pairs at FDR < 0.05. That said, if we filter our results to look our top EWAS hits that do carry an eQTM, we see that the nearest-gene and effector-gene can differ:

Code 
# The twelve rows rendered below: the best-ranked hits that carry an eQTM.
eqd <- annotated[!is.na(BIOS_eQTM_genes)][1:12]
# Is the effector gene also the nearest gene? TRUE when any eQTM gene appears in
# the probe's own (semicolon-separated) gene list. mapply because both sides are
# strings that have to be split row by row.
eqd[, nearest := fifelse(mapply(function(g, e) {
      if (is.na(g) || g == "") return(FALSE)
      any(strsplit(e, ";")[[1]] %in% strsplit(g, ";")[[1]])
    }, genesUniq, BIOS_eQTM_genes), "yes", "no")]
eqdisp <- eqd[, .(probe,
                  nearest_gene = fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq == "", "-", genesUniq),
                  eQTM_gene = BIOS_eQTM_genes, `nearest?` = nearest,
                  eQTM_FDR = signif(BIOS_eQTM_minFDR, 3),
                  bacon_p = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(eqdisp, "data/08_annotation/eqtm_display.csv")

# the same hits, untrimmed and with every annotation column, for anyone who
# wants to look further down the ranking than the table below shows
fwrite(annotated[!is.na(BIOS_eQTM_genes)][1:200],
       "data/08_annotation/eqtm_top_hits.csv")

For cg12218747 the nearest genes are CBR1-AS1/SETD4, but the CpG’s methylation tracks the expression of CBR1. For cg26713179 the nearest gene is ZNF766 while the eQTM points at the neighboring ZNF528/ZNF880 cluster. Four of these twelve hits show an effector that differs from the nearest gene. When reporting results, the effector gene is usually the one people want to know about if the information is available.

Part 2 — Region-level analysis (DMRs)

Why look at regions at all

Single-CpG EWAS tests each probe independently, but methylation is not evenly spaced throughout the genome, and methylation arrays tend to target CpG islands and gene promotor regions where there are likely to be multiple methylation sites close together. Methylation sites in close proximity to each other are likely to have the same methylation status. A region with several unmethylated CpGs is a stronger biological indicator that is an actively expressed region than a single unmethylated CpG, and vice versa for methylated regions. This phenomenon in statistics is called spatial autocorrelation. A cluster of five or six adjacent CpGs each at p ≈ 10⁻⁴ when tested individually (not reaching statistical significance in an EWAS) is, collectively, a statistically significant region.

DMR tools

The choice of DMR tool is constrained by what upstream modeling you did.

Importantcomb-p works on summary statistics; DMRcate needs line-level data

comb-p (Pedersen et al. 2012) takes only a BED-style formatted file of per-CpG p-values and coordinates. It never sees the samples or line-level methylation or phenotype data. That means it works downstream of any EWAS model, however complex. If your analysis plan involves stratification and meta-analysis, comb-p is the tool to use. This is why the Snakemake pipeline uses comb-p.

DMRcate (Peters et al. 2015) takes line-level β/M values plus a single design formula and re-fits the model internally to compute a smoothed, region-level statistic. It is powerful and self-contained, but it cannot consume meta-analyzed results — there is no single design matrix that represents “stratify by sex, then inverse-variance meta-analyze.” If you used the stratified-meta workflow, DMRcate is not an option; if you fit one pooled model with sex as a covariate, it is.

Running comb-p on our EWAS results

comb-p’s pipeline command chains four steps: estimate the spatial autocorrelation function (ACF) of the p-values, use it to compute autocorrelation-adjusted regional p-values (the Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris correction), FDR-correct those, and finally stitch adjacent low-p CpGs into regions. First we write the BED (this is the pipeline’s make_bed.R). The p-values come straight from the chapter 06 BACON fit; the coordinates come from the same Zhou v8.1 hg38 release the chapter 03 mask came from, so the BED and the mask cannot drift apart:

NoteWhat this section needs

This section starts from data/06_ewas.rds, written by chapter 06. If you did not run that chapter, fetch the published checkpoint instead:

Terminal
./get_data.sh F_ewas_results

It also needs the probe-order and hg38 coordinate tables from the same Zhou v8.1 release chapter 03 used. You do not need to fetch either: the probe ordering is the copy chapter 03 already committed under data/, and the coordinate table is read directly from the Zhou lab’s repository in the chunk below.

Code 
# This chunk writes the file comb-p needs for input.
tt  <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/06_ewas.rds")$tt)
# The YAME probe order and the coordinate table are two halves of one file pair:
# row i of the coordinate table is the probe named on row i of the ordering
# file, which is why they are assembled side by side and not merged.
# The ordering is the same committed file chapter 03 reads. The coordinate table
# (5 MB) is downloaded from the zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotation repository, pinned to a
# commit so it cannot change underneath the ordering it has to line up with.
ord <- fread("data/EPIC.ordering.tsv.gz", select = "Probe_ID")    # YAME probe order
crd <- fread(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotation/",
                    "e91f9e992cc60f2f52f15c564e359ac6718d4cfd/EPIC/EPIC.hg38.coord.tsv.gz"))
                                                                   # same order, one row per probe
map <- data.table(probe = ord$Probe_ID,
                  CpG_chrm = crd$CpG_chrm, CpG_beg = crd$CpG_beg)

bed <- merge(tt, map, by = "probe")[
  # comb-p walks ordered positions along a chromosome, so keep the assembled
  # chromosomes only: a probe on a scaffold has no neighbors to borrow from
  grepl("^chr([0-9]+|X|Y)$", CpG_chrm),
  # comb-p's column contract: chrom/start/end, the p-value it smooths, and an
  # id it carries through untouched. The '#' on the first name is what makes
  # the header a comment line to the tool.
  .(`#chrom` = CpG_chrm, start = CpG_beg, end = CpG_beg + 2L,
    pvals = bacon.p, cpgid = probe)]
setorder(bed, `#chrom`, start)
fwrite(bed, "data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed", sep = "\t")

That writes 756,234 of the 756,251 tested CpGs — the 17 that fall on unplaced or alt contigs are dropped, because comb-p works on ordered positions along a chromosome and a scaffold has no neighbors to borrow from.

Then the region detection, with the pipeline’s default parameters (config.yml: min_pvalue = 1e-4, window_size = 200, region_filter = 0.05):

comb-p is a Python tool with its own environment (conda env create -f envs/combp.yml); run the command below in a terminal from the tutorial/ folder. Its seven output files are committed under data/08_annotation/dmr/, so the R chunks that follow run whether or not you run it. --seed is the p-value a CpG must reach to start a region, and --dist is how far apart (in bp) neighbouring CpGs can be and still extend it:

Terminal
mkdir -p data/08_annotation/dmr
comb-p pipeline \
    --seed 1e-4 \
    --dist 200 \
    --region-filter-p 0.05 \
    -p data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr \
    data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed

That one command writes seven files, all sharing the -p prefix. Nothing prints the answer to screen, so it is worth knowing which file holds what:

file contents
PTSD_dmr.args.txt the exact invocation, the comb-p version, and the run date — keep this for your methods section
PTSD_dmr.acf.txt the fitted autocorrelation function: lag_min, lag_max, correlation, N, p
PTSD_dmr.slk.bed.gz every input CpG with its smoothed regional p: #chrom, start, end, p (your input p), region-p (SLK-smoothed)
PTSD_dmr.fdr.bed.gz the same rows plus region-q, the Benjamini–Hochberg correction of region-p
PTSD_dmr.regions.bed.gz the stitched regions, minimal and headerless: chrom, start, end, min_p, n_probes
PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz the regions with statistics: #chrom, start, end, min_p, n_probes, z_p, z_sidak_p
PTSD_dmr.regions-t.bed the regions that pass --region-filter-p — here the single region with z_sidak_p < 0.05

regions-p.bed.gz is the file to read: it lists every candidate region with both the uncorrected and the Šidák-corrected region p. regions-t.bed is that same table filtered down to what survived, which makes it the convenient endpoint for a pipeline. In this run the two files carry identical columns because our input BED has no effect-size column for comb-p to carry through.

The ACF step reports short-range autocorrelation in our p-values (correlation ≈ 0.054 out to ~71 bp, p ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻¹²⁸ over 202,078 CpG pairs). Methylation is spatially structured here, as expected. The SLK/FDR steps then propose two candidate regions, and one of them survives the Šidák correction for the number of regions tested:

region (hg38) n CpGs min_p z_sidak_p
chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701 11 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶
chr3:138,608,544–138,608,573 2 9.3 × 10⁻⁵ 0.53

Those are five of the seven columns in regions-p.bed.gz — the three coordinate columns are collapsed into one here, and z_p is omitted (it is the Šidák-uncorrected region p, 3.3 × 10⁻²⁰ for the chr6 region). The surviving region sits at chr6:28.63 Mb, inside the MHC/HLA region.

Warningmin_p in the comb-p output is not a raw probe p-value

The region above is reported with min_p = 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ and z_sidak_p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶. Despite the column name, that min_p is not the smallest input p-value in the region: it is the smallest Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris–smoothed, FDR-corrected regional q among the region’s CpGs (the raw SLK p at those same CpGs goes down to 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁹). Smoothing pools each CpG with its neighbors, so these values are orders of magnitude below anything in the input: the smallest raw BACON p among the eleven CpGs is 1.1 × 10⁻⁵, and the smallest anywhere in the BED is 2.0 × 10⁻⁷. Smoothed regional statistics and probe-level statistics are not on the same scale, and comparing them directly will make a region look far stronger than the data supporting it.

ImportantSet the seed threshold on purpose

--seed is the p-value a CpG must reach before comb-p will even start a region there; --dist then decides how far the region may extend. The seed is not a significance threshold for the result — the Šidák-corrected region p is — so setting it at genome-wide-significance levels defeats the point of doing region analysis at all. The default of 1 × 10⁻⁴ finds the MHC region above. If your DMR run comes back empty, you can adjust the seed p-value to something less stringent, but make sure you have a reason to justify the p-value you do use!

TipThe MHC is a blood-EWAS landmark

That the strongest regional signal falls in the MHC on chromosome 6. The MHC is one of the most gene-dense and polymorphic regions of the human genome, and it is associated with more diseases than any other region (Horton et al. 2004). It also surfaces in many blood EWAS. It is simultaneously the region where you should be most cautious about SNP-driven artifacts. We already removed common-SNP-affected sites, but it is possible that rare variants, structural variants, or undocumented genetic variation is driving this signal. Further causal inference testing with genetic or gene expression data can help clarify why we are seeing this signal in the MHC.

Show the code for the DMR locus plot 
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

# The strongest comb-p region, by Sidak-corrected p, from the file the command above wrote
lead <- fread("data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz")[order(z_sidak_p)][1]
lead_chr <- lead[[1]]; lead_start <- lead$start; lead_end <- lead$end

# Every tested CpG within 2.5 kb of the region, with its BACON p-value and hg38 position
ann_loc <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/08_annotation/annotated.rds"))
bonf_line <- -log10(0.05 / nrow(ann_loc))
loc <- ann_loc[CpG_chrm == lead_chr &
               CpG_beg >= lead_start - 2500 & CpG_beg <= lead_end + 2500]
loc[, in_region := CpG_beg >= lead_start & CpG_beg <= lead_end]

ggplot(loc, aes(CpG_beg / 1e6, -log10(bacon.p), colour = in_region)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = lead_start / 1e6, xmax = lead_end / 1e6,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#1A6B75", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = CpG_beg / 1e6, y = 0, yend = -log10(bacon.p))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bonf_line, colour = "#8C3A4A") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1A6B75", `FALSE` = "gray60"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = paste0(lead_chr, " position (Mb, hg38)"),
       y = expression(-log[10]~italic(p)[BACON]))

ENmix::combp: the same method, but with R

comb-p is a Python command-line tool, which means an extra environment to install for one step of one chapter. If you would rather stay in R, ENmix::combp (Xu et al. 2021) implements the same Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris approach, and it takes the BED we just built with only a column rename. (The same package also offers ipdmr (Xu et al. 2020), the authors’ interval-p-value variant.)

NoteWhat this section needs

This section starts from data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed, written by the make-bed chunk above. If you did not run that chunk, fetch the published copy instead:

Terminal
./get_data.sh H_annotation
Code 
# ENmix's R implementation of the comb-p algorithm. The Python comb-p it is
# compared against below lives in `envs/combp.yml`.
library(ENmix)

bed <- data.table::fread("data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed")
# ENmix expects its own column names, in this order
data.table::setnames(bed, c("chr", "start", "end", "p", "probe"))
bed <- as.data.frame(bed)          # ENmix wants a plain data.frame
bed$chr <- as.character(bed$chr)

combp(data = bed,
      dist.cutoff = 750,           # must exceed bin.size (see the warning below)
      bin.size    = 310,           # ACF bin width
      seed        = 1e-4,          # FDR threshold for seeding a region
      nCores      = 4,
      region_plot = FALSE, mht_plot = FALSE)
P value correlations:
      bin         acf
0.cor 310 0.041191117
1.cor 620 0.015511265
2.cor 750 0.005481039
Number of DMRs identified:   9
Code 
# combp() always writes resu_combp.csv into the working directory; move it
# alongside the other chapter 08 outputs
file.rename("resu_combp.csv", "data/08_annotation/08_enmix_combp.csv")
[1] TRUE
Code 
enmix <- data.table::fread("data/08_annotation/08_enmix_combp.csv")
cat("ENmix regions:", nrow(enmix), "| Sidak < 0.05:", sum(enmix$sidak < 0.05), "\n")
ENmix regions: 9 | Sidak < 0.05: 7
Code 
enmix[which.min(enmix$sidak), .(chr, start, end, nprobe, sidak)]

It runs in about a minute on our 756,234-row BED and finds the same lead region: a 12-CpG DMR at chr6:28,633,494–28,633,743, the MHC-proximal locus command-line comb-p reports as 11 CpGs at chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701. The probe lists overlap almost completely; ENmix extends the region by one CpG (cg12763978) at the 3′ end.

WarningTwo ways this differs from the command-line tool:

bin.size must be smaller than dist.cutoff. ENmix builds its autocorrelation bins by seq(bin.size, dist.cutoff, bin.size), so calling it with the shipped command-line settings (--dist 200 with the default bin.size = 310) fails with wrong sign in 'by' argument rather than a message naming the problem. The dist.cutoff = 750 above is chosen to exceed the default bin width.

The two implementations do not return the same region count. With the settings above ENmix reports 9 candidate regions of which 7 clear Šidák < 0.05, where command-line comb-p at --dist 200 --seed 1e-4 reports 2 candidates of which 1 clears Šidák. Both single out the same chr6 locus as by far the strongest — ENmix calls 12 CpGs there against comb-p’s 11 — but ENmix is much more permissive about everything else. Some of that is the wider dist.cutoff, and some is that ENmix describes itself as a modified comb-p. Treat it as an R-native implementation of the same idea. Either method is okay, just make sure to report which one you used and its parameters.

The DMR numbers in this chapter come from the command-line tool at the parameters shown above, which is what chapter 07’s pipeline invokes.

DMRcate: the line-level alternative

If you are using DMRcate, it operates on the M-value matrix directly:

Generic example, do not run
# Schematic only: `M` and `design` are yours to supply. This chapter does not run
# DMRcate: it needs the full M-value matrix and the chapter 06 design in memory,
# and the pipeline's stratified route has no single design matrix to hand it.
library(DMRcate)
# M = CpG x sample matrix; design = model.matrix(~ PTSD + sex + age + cellcounts + SVs)
myannotation <- cpg.annotate("array", M, arraytype = "EPICv1",
                             analysis.type = "differential",
                             design = design, coef = "PTSD")
dmrs <- dmrcate(myannotation, lambda = 1000, C = 2)   # Gaussian-kernel smoothing
results.ranges <- extractRanges(dmrs, genome = "hg19")  # EPICv1 annotation is hg19,
                                                          # unlike this chapter's hg38 regions

Note what it requires that comb-p does not: the full M matrix in memory and a single design/coef. If your EWAS was residualized or meta-analyzed, you cannot express it as one coef here.

Annotating the DMRs

Once regions exist, the pipeline’s dmr_annotation.R maps each DMR back to genes and islands by overlapping its coordinates against three UCSC hg38 tables: refGene, cpgIslandExt, and the HGNC gene track. The chunk below downloads the same three from UCSC. The DMR’s constituent CpGs are looked up by coordinate in the Part 1 annotation table (annotated.rds), so each region carries its probe list and direction of effect. The overlap is a coordinate join — bedtools intersect in the pipeline, or GenomicRanges::findOverlaps() if you are staying in R — with no modeling involved. We run it here for our one region, the eleven CpGs of the comb-p MHC region at chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701:

Code 
library(GenomicRanges)   # GRanges(), IRanges(), overlapsAny(), nearest()
library(jsonlite)        # fromJSON(), for the UCSC API query below

# The comb-p DMR, in hg38: the region with the smallest Sidak-corrected p in the
# regions-p file the comb-p command above wrote
top_dmr <- fread("data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz")[order(z_sidak_p)][1]
dmr <- GRanges(top_dmr[[1]], IRanges(top_dmr$start, top_dmr$end))

# The same three UCSC hg38 tables the pipeline's fetch_dmr_annotation_cache rule
# downloads. refGene and cpgIslandExt are plain gzipped tables, so fread() reads
# them straight from the UCSC download server.
ucsc <- "https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/database/"

# refGene: columns 3-6 are chrom, strand, txStart, txEnd; column 13 is the gene symbol
rg <- fread(paste0(ucsc, "refGene.txt.gz"), header = FALSE, select = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 13),
            col.names = c("chrom", "strand", "txStart", "txEnd", "gene"))
refGene <- GRanges(rg$chrom, IRanges(rg$txStart + 1L, rg$txEnd),   # UCSC starts are 0-based
                   strand = rg$strand, gene = rg$gene)

# cpgIslandExt: columns 2-4 are chrom, chromStart, chromEnd
cgi <- fread(paste0(ucsc, "cpgIslandExt.txt.gz"), header = FALSE, select = 2:4,
             col.names = c("chrom", "chromStart", "chromEnd"))
cpgIslands <- GRanges(cgi$chrom, IRanges(cgi$chromStart + 1L, cgi$chromEnd))

# The HGNC track is a bigBed (the pipeline converts it with bigBedToBed). R's
# bigBed reader cannot parse this file's colour column, so ask the UCSC API for
# the records overlapping the DMR instead (API coordinates are 0-based).
hgnc <- fromJSON(paste0("https://api.genome.ucsc.edu/getData/track?genome=hg38;track=hgnc;",
                        sprintf("chrom=%s;start=%d;end=%d", as.character(seqnames(dmr)),
                                start(dmr) - 1L, end(dmr))))$hgnc

# genes whose transcript lies within 5 kb of the DMR, and the nearest one on each side
near_ref <- refGene[overlapsAny(refGene, dmr + 5000)]
lower    <- refGene[follow(dmr, refGene, ignore.strand = TRUE)]
higher   <- refGene[precede(dmr, refGene, ignore.strand = TRUE)]
length(near_ref)
[1] 0
Code 
data.frame(side = c("lower coordinate", "higher coordinate"),
           gene = c(lower$gene, higher$gene),
           distance_bp = c(distance(dmr, lower), distance(dmr, higher)))
Code 
hgnc[, c("symbol", "geneName", "locus_type")]
Code 
# nearest CpG island: within 2 kb counts as a shore
isl <- cpgIslands[nearest(dmr, cpgIslands)]
distance(dmr, isl)
[1] 1375

This is a prime example region because the three annotation sources disagree, and the pipeline’s default gene table is the one that comes up empty. While often the sources do agree, it is not uncommon for annotation disagreements to occur:

Code 
# One row per annotation source: what each names for the DMR. Rows one and two
# come from the UCSC queries in the chunk above; row three from the GENCODE v41
# annotation built in Part 1 (annotated.rds).
ann <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/08_annotation/annotated.rds"))
# the region's CpGs by coordinate, not by a pasted probe list, so the region
# definition lives in one place
reg <- ann[CpG_chrm == as.character(seqnames(dmr)) &
           CpG_beg >= start(dmr) & CpG_beg <= end(dmr)]
setorder(reg, CpG_beg)
stopifnot(nrow(reg) == top_dmr$n_probes)   # the count comb-p reported; fail loudly if the map changed

# every gencode v41 gene the eleven probes are assigned to, de-duplicated
gencode_genes <- paste(sort(unique(unlist(strsplit(reg$genesUniq, ";")))),
                       collapse = ", ")

dmr_src <- data.table(
  `Annotation source` = c("UCSC refGene (pipeline default gene table)",
                          "UCSC HGNC track",
                          "Zhou GENCODE v41 (our probe-level annotation)"),
  names = c(
    if (length(near_ref) == 0)
      sprintf("nothing within \u00b15 kb (nearest %s ~%.0f kb, %s ~%.0f kb)",
              lower$gene, distance(dmr, lower) / 1000, higher$gene, distance(dmr, higher) / 1000)
    else paste(unique(near_ref$gene), collapse = ", "),
    paste0(hgnc$symbol, " (", hgnc$geneName, ", directly overlapping)"),
    paste0(gencode_genes, " (promoter-associated, non-coding)")))
# the second column is labelled with the region's own hg38 coordinates
setnames(dmr_src, "names",
         sprintf("What it names for %s:%s\u2013%s", as.character(seqnames(dmr)),
                 formatC(start(dmr), big.mark = ",", format = "d"),
                 formatC(end(dmr),   big.mark = ",", format = "d")))
fwrite(dmr_src, "data/08_annotation/dmr_source_comparison.csv")
Code 
# written by the `dmr-sources-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/dmr_source_comparison.csv"),
  caption = "Three hg38 gene annotations, three answers for the same DMR. refGene — the pipeline's default `gene_table` — names nothing nearby; the region only acquires a label from the pseudogene track or from GENCODE.")
Three hg38 gene annotations, three answers for the same DMR. refGene — the pipeline’s default gene_table — names nothing nearby; the region only acquires a label from the pseudogene track or from GENCODE.
Annotation source What it names for chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701
UCSC refGene (pipeline default gene table) nothing within ±5 kb (nearest ZBED9 ~17 kb, LINC00533 ~15 kb)
UCSC HGNC track COX8CP1 (COX8C pseudogene 1, directly overlapping)
Zhou GENCODE v41 (our probe-level annotation) ENSG00000271440, ENSG00000287279 (promoter-associated, non-coding)

refGene is a curated set of well-supported transcripts, so a DMR sitting in a gene-poor stretch of the MHC returns nothing within 5 kb — the nearest curated genes (ZBED9, LINC00533) are >14 kb away. The HGNC BigBed, which includes pseudogenes and genes from difficult to map regions, overlaps COX8CP1 directly, and our probe-level GENCODE v41 annotation assigns the CpGs to two non-coding transcripts as promoter hits. None of these is “wrong”; they reflect different inclusion criteria. The lesson for a DMR walkthrough is to read the coordinates, not just the gene symbol: an empty gene_table overlap does not mean the region is intergenic junk — here it is a CpG-island shore over a pseudogene in an immune-gene-dense locus, exactly the kind of place methylation differences cluster. Our eleven CpGs, all hypomethylated in cases, look like this:

Code 
# The eleven-row table rendered below, and the fuller per-CpG file that backs
# it. Both come from `reg` — the region's CpGs in the Part 1 annotation layer,
# built in the chunk above.
disp <- reg[, .(CpG = probe,
                `hg38 position (chr6)` = formatC(CpG_beg, big.mark = ",", format = "d"),
                # the annotation layer's label is "Promoter (±1.5 kb TSS)";
                # trim the parenthetical so the column stays narrow
                `GENCODE feature` = sub(" \\(.*", "", feature),
                `CGI context` = island,
                # β difference on the 0-1 scale: -0.022 reads as 2.2 points hypo
                `Δβ (case − control)` = round(delta_beta, 3),
                `BACON p` = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(disp, "data/08_annotation/dmr_cpg_display.csv")

# the same eleven CpGs with everything the annotation layer knows about them,
# including the transcript list the display table has no room for
full <- reg[, .(probe, CpG_beg, CpG_end, genesUniq, transcriptTypes, distTSS,
                feature, island, BIOS_eQTM_genes,
                delta_beta = round(delta_beta, 4),
                bacon.es   = round(bacon.es, 3),
                bacon.p    = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(full, "data/08_annotation/dmr_cpg_annotation.csv")

From regions to pathways: goregion

The gene-set tools in Part 3 take a list of CpGs. When your unit of discovery is a region, missMethyl::goregion (Phipson et al. 2016) is the region-level analog of gometh: give it a GRanges of your DMRs and it maps each region to the CpGs it contains, collapses those to genes, and runs the same probe-number-bias-corrected GO/KEGG test. It is the natural way to ask “are my comb-p regions collectively enriched for a biological process?”

By default goregion (like gometh in Part 3) uses Illumina’s hg19 annotation package to decide which CpGs fall in a region and which genes they belong to, whereas the rest of this chapter, including the comb-p region itself, uses Wanding Zhou’s hg38 resources. Both functions accept an annotation of your own through their anno argument, so we build one from the Zhou GENCODE v41 manifest read in Part 1. missMethyl expects the column names of Illumina’s package, so the Zhou columns are renamed to match:

Code 
# One row per CpG probe with hg38 coordinates. `v41` is the Zhou manifest read in Part 1.
z <- v41[grepl("^cg", probeID) & !is.na(CpG_beg)]
genes <- fifelse(is.na(z$genesUniq), "", z$genesUniq)     # ';'-separated gene names
zhou_anno <- S4Vectors::DataFrame(
  Name   = z$probeID,
  chr    = z$CpG_chrm,
  pos    = z$CpG_beg + 1L,                                # Zhou's starts are 0-based
  strand = fifelse(is.na(z$probe_strand), "*", z$probe_strand),
  UCSC_RefGene_Name = genes,
  # missMethyl wants one gene-region label per gene. It only uses them when you
  # restrict the test to particular regions (genomic.features), which we do not,
  # so a placeholder label is enough.
  UCSC_RefGene_Group = vapply(strsplit(genes, ";"),
                              function(g) paste(rep("gene", length(g)), collapse = ";"), ""),
  row.names = z$probeID)
nrow(zhou_anno)
[1] 862927
Code 
library(missMethyl)
# The DMR from its eleven CpGs' hg38 positions. `reg` is the region's rows of the
# Part 1 annotation, built in the dmr-sources-derive chunk above.
dmr_gr <- GenomicRanges::reduce(GenomicRanges::GRanges(
  reg$CpG_chrm, IRanges::IRanges(reg$CpG_beg + 1L, width = 2)))

# all.cpg is the tested universe: `tt` is the chapter 06 top-table read in by the
# make-bed chunk above
gr_go <- goregion(dmr_gr, all.cpg = tt$probe, collection = "GO",
                  array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno)
Error in `getMappedEntrezIDs()`:
! There are no genes annotated to the significant CpGs

Run on our single MHC DMR, goregion returns an error: “There are no genes annotated to the significant CpGs.”. In Zhou’s GENCODE v41 annotation the region’s CpGs are assigned only to two unnamed non-coding genes, which have Ensembl IDs but no gene symbol. missMethyl can only test genes it can match to an Entrez ID, so there is nothing to map to a GO term. (Illumina’s hg19 annotation gives the same error for this region.) Two lessons fall out of this:

  1. Enrichment inherits the annotation’s gene assignments. If the annotation maps a region to no gene, a gene-centric lens for pathway enrichment will not have anything to query or report.
  2. goregion needs many regions to be meaningful. One region is never an “enrichment”; a real DMR analysis feeds it the dozens-to-hundreds of regions comb-p or DMRcate returns genome-wide. We show the mechanism here even though it doesn’t produce a meaningful result so the call is in your toolkit.

Part 3 — Pathway, trait, and functional enrichment

Annotation names the genes near your hits; enrichment asks whether that gene list is collectively over-represented in any biological process, pathway, or previously reported trait. This is where an EWAS stops being a list of CpGs and starts pointing at mechanism. Two things make methylation enrichment different from the gene-expression version you may know:

  1. Probe-number bias. Genes are not covered evenly on the array — a large gene like PRKG1 carries hundreds of probes, a small one only a handful. A naive test that treats “gene has ≥1 significant CpG” as a hit will therefore flag long, densely-tiled genes purely because they had more chances to be picked. Enrichment for methylation must correct for the number of probes per gene.
  2. Multiple CpGs map to one gene, and CpGs in intergenic space map to none. The tool has to collapse probes to genes sensibly before testing.

missMethyl gometh: the reproducible, bias-corrected default

missMethyl::gometh() (and its generic gsameth() for custom gene sets) is the field-standard R implementation. It maps your significant CpGs to genes, models the per-gene probe count as the bias covariate, and runs a corrected hypergeometric test against GO or KEGG (Phipson et al. 2016). By default it assigns CpGs to genes with Illumina’s hg19 EPIC annotation package; passing anno = zhou_anno makes it use the same Zhou hg38 GENCODE v41 genes as the rest of this chapter. Enrichment has not yet been added to the Snakemake pipeline, but will in a future release.

Normally you would run GO/KEGG enrichment only on the CpGs that reach epigenome-wide significance. The EWAS of this subset identified none, which leaves nothing to test, so here we use the top 1,000 CpGs by BACON p-value as our “significant set”.

Code 
# The Wallenius test runs over every GO term, so this takes about a minute. The
# RDS written at the end is what the comparison table further down reads.
# `zhou_anno` is the hg38 annotation built in Part 2's zhou-anno chunk.
library(missMethyl)
tt     <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
all.cpg <- tt$probe                          # tested universe = every CpG you analyzed
sig.cpg <- tt[order(bacon.p)][1:1000]$probe  # your significant set

# GO enrichment, corrected for probes-per-gene. array.type matches your array.
# anno = zhou_anno: genes from Zhou's hg38 GENCODE v41, not Illumina's hg19 default
go <- gometh(sig.cpg = sig.cpg, all.cpg = all.cpg,
             collection = "GO", array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno,
             plot.bias = TRUE)
Code 
go <- go[order(go$P.DE), ]

# KEGG is a one-word change
kegg <- gometh(sig.cpg = sig.cpg, all.cpg = all.cpg,
               collection = "KEGG", array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno)
kegg <- kegg[order(kegg$P.DE), ]

# Both collections in one object. The method comparison below reads `kegg` back
# out of it, and keeping `go` alongside means the GO panel of the figure can be
# redrawn without re-running the test.
saveRDS(list(go = go, kegg = kegg), "data/08_annotation/08_gometh.rds")

Two arguments carry all the weight. all.cpg is the full tested set — it must be every CpG that survived your QC and filtering, not the whole array manifest, or the test is biased toward whatever your pipeline happened to remove. plot.bias = TRUE draws the probe-number bias curve; glance at it once to confirm the correction is actually engaging. Defining “significant” by a fixed top-N (here 1,000) is a teaching compromise, as noted above.

Run on our teaching subset, the corrected results are:

Code 
top_terms <- rbind(
  data.table(collection = "GO",   term = head(go$TERM, 10),          DE = head(go$DE, 10),
             N = head(go$N, 10),   p = head(go$P.DE, 10)),
  data.table(collection = "KEGG", term = head(kegg$Description, 10), DE = head(kegg$DE, 10),
             N = head(kegg$N, 10), p = head(kegg$P.DE, 10)))
top_terms[, term := factor(term, levels = rev(unique(term)))]
ggplot(top_terms, aes(x = -log10(p), y = term)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1A6B75") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(DE, "/", N)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ collection, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = expression(-log[10]~italic(P)[DE]~"(nominal)"), y = NULL)

The top nominal terms here are zonula adherens (GO:0005915, P = 1.6 × 10⁻³), the catenin-TCF7L2 complex, regulation of syncytium formation by plasma membrane fusion, and cell-cell adhesion. It is easy to read a cell-adhesion theme into that list, but there is no term at FDR < 0.05 in either collection. The smallest FDR in both GO and KEGG is 1 (the top KEGG pathway is Adherens junction, nominal P = 0.0032). This is exactly what enrichment of a null gene list should look like. Reading this result as “PTSD methylation remodels adherens junctions” would be false: with 1,000 arbitrarily-chosen CpGs, a handful of small gene sets always reach nominal p < 0.01 by chance — note that the leading GO term has only 8 genes in it, 4 of which the top set touched.

methylGSA: the same question, a different bias model

gometh is not the only way to correct for the probe-number bias, and the choice of correction can change the outcome. methylGSA (Ren and Kuan 2019) offers two alternatives to gometh’s Wallenius hypergeometric test. By default it uses Illumina’s hg19 annotation package; its FullAnnot argument takes a CpG-to-gene table of your own, so we give it the same Zhou hg38 GENCODE v41 genes gometh used. The three methods below then differ in their statistics, not their gene assignments:

  • methylglm models each gene set with a logistic regression in which the per-gene number of probes enters as a covariate — a continuous adjustment rather than a weighted urn, and it takes the whole ranked p-value vector, not a hard top-N cutoff.
  • methylRRA aggregates the CpG p-values to a per-gene score by robust rank aggregation, then runs either an over-representation test or a GSEA-style rank test — no significance cutoff at all.
NoteThis section runs in its own environment

On the R-only route, BiocManager installs methylGSA alongside everything else and there is nothing to do. Conda users need envs/methylgsa.yml (conda env create -f envs/methylgsa.yml) because bioconda’s newest methylGSA build is for an older R than the rest of the stack. Nothing is shared at run time: the only input below is the BACON top-table CSV written by chapter 06. Copy the chunk into a script and run it from the tutorial/ folder with conda run -n methylgsa Rscript <script>; it writes the three files the comparison chunks below read. Those three files are also committed to the repository, so the rest of the section runs without this step.

Code 
library(methylGSA)
library(data.table)   # fread()/fwrite()

# This chunk runs in its own R session, so it reads the Zhou v41 manifest itself.
# prepareAnnot() wants one row per CpG: the probe ID and its ';'-separated genes.
v41 <- fread(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotationData/",
                    "6d176d6e7e56465403d4478a09fe11b983eeb721/Anno/EPIC/",
                    "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz"))
cpg2gene  <- v41[grepl("^cg", probeID) & !is.na(genesUniq) & genesUniq != "",
                 .(CpG = probeID, gene = genesUniq)]
FullAnnot <- prepareAnnot(as.data.frame(cpg2gene))

tt <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
pv <- setNames(tt$bacon.p, tt$probe)          # NAMED vector: names = CpG IDs

# logistic-regression enrichment (bias covariate = probes per gene)
mglm <- methylglm(cpg.pval = pv, FullAnnot = FullAnnot,
                  GS.type = "KEGG", minsize = 10, maxsize = 500)

# GSEA on rank-aggregated per-gene scores. Its p-values come from random
# permutations, so fix the seed to get the same table on every run.
set.seed(20260922)
mrra <- methylRRA(cpg.pval = pv, FullAnnot = FullAnnot, method = "GSEA",
                  GS.type = "KEGG", minsize = 10, maxsize = 500)

# methylGSA looks pathway names up through clusterProfiler, whose older releases
# no longer get human pathway IDs back from KEGG, leaving Description empty. Fill
# any gaps from KEGG's own list of human pathways.
kegg_names <- fread("https://rest.kegg.jp/list/pathway/hsa", header = FALSE,
                    col.names = c("id", "name"))
kegg_names[, `:=`(id = sub("^hsa", "", id), name = sub(" - Homo sapiens \\(human\\)$", "", name))]
fill_names <- function(res) {
  miss <- is.na(res$Description)
  res$Description[miss] <- kegg_names$name[match(res$ID[miss], kegg_names$id)]
  res
}
mglm <- fill_names(mglm)
mrra <- fill_names(mrra)

# Export results
saveRDS(list(methylglm = mglm, methylRRA = mrra),
        "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa.rds")
glm_top <- head(as.data.table(mglm)[order(pvalue)], 10)[
  , .(Method = "methylglm", KEGG = ID, Pathway = Description, Size, pvalue, padj)]
fwrite(glm_top, "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_glm_top.csv")
rra_top <- head(as.data.table(mrra)[order(pvalue)], 5)[
  , .(Method = "methylRRA-GSEA", KEGG = ID, Pathway = Description, Size,
      NES, pvalue, padj)]
fwrite(rra_top, "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv")

We ran all three tools on the same BACON top-table, against the same KEGG collection, and recorded both how many pathways each calls significant at FDR < 0.05 and what each one puts at the top:

Code 
# The comparison table rendered below, rebuilt from the three result files the
# two chunks above write rather than typed out by hand.
g  <- readRDS("data/08_annotation/08_gometh.rds")
kg <- as.data.table(g$kegg, keep.rownames = "ID")[order(P.DE)]
# KEGG ids are zero-padded ("04140"), so they must not be read as integers.
gl <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_glm_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
rr <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
mg <- readRDS("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa.rds")   # full methylglm and methylRRA tables

# A misspelled column name returns NULL, which c() drops without warning; the
# two remaining names would then be recycled down three rows. Check first.
leaders <- c(kg$Description[1], gl$Pathway[1], rr$Pathway[1])
stopifnot(length(leaders) == 3L)

cmp <- data.table(
  Method = c("gometh (Wallenius hypergeometric)",
             "methylglm (logistic regression)",
             "methylRRA-GSEA (rank aggregation)"),
  Input  = c("top 1,000 CpGs vs universe",
             "full named p-value vector",
             "full named p-value vector"),
  `Bias model` = c("probes per gene (Wallenius)",
                   "probe count as covariate",
                   "gene-level RRA score"),
  # The two methylGSA top files hold only their top rows, so the significant
  # counts are taken from the full result tables in 08_methylgsa.rds.
  `KEGG FDR<0.05` = c(sum(kg$FDR < 0.05),
                      sum(mg$methylglm$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                      sum(mg$methylRRA$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
  `Top KEGG pathway` = leaders,
  `Its nominal p` = signif(c(kg$P.DE[1], gl$pvalue[1], rr$pvalue[1]), 3),
  `Its FDR`       = signif(c(kg$FDR[1],  gl$padj[1],   rr$padj[1]),   3)
)
fwrite(cmp, "data/08_annotation/08_gsa_method_comparison.csv")
Code 
# written by the `gsa-compare-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/08_gsa_method_comparison.csv"),
  caption = "Three probe-bias corrections, one dataset, one gene annotation (Zhou hg38 GENCODE v41). gometh and methylglm return no KEGG pathway at FDR < 0.05; methylRRA-GSEA returns eight. Each nominates a different pathway as its leader — the ranking, not just the count, depends on the bias model and the input convention.")
Three probe-bias corrections, one dataset, one gene annotation (Zhou hg38 GENCODE v41). gometh and methylglm return no KEGG pathway at FDR < 0.05; methylRRA-GSEA returns eight. Each nominates a different pathway as its leader — the ranking, not just the count, depends on the bias model and the input convention.
Method Input Bias model KEGG FDR<0.05 Top KEGG pathway Its nominal p Its FDR
gometh (Wallenius hypergeometric) top 1,000 CpGs vs universe probes per gene (Wallenius) 0 Adherens junction 0.003180 1.0000
methylglm (logistic regression) full named p-value vector probe count as covariate 0 Amoebiasis 0.003400 0.6250
methylRRA-GSEA (rank aggregation) full named p-value vector gene-level RRA score 8 Non-small cell lung cancer 0.000201 0.0263

The three tools use the same genes and the same pathways, and still disagree. gometh and methylglm find nothing at FDR < 0.05, with smallest FDRs of 1 and 0.63, while methylRRA-GSEA reports eight significant pathways, led by Non-small cell lung cancer and Pyruvate metabolism (both FDR = 0.026). Each also nominates a different leader (Adherens junction, Amoebiasis, Non-small cell lung cancer).

Treat those eight pathways methylRRA identifies with caution. methylRRA’s GSEA mode uses the full ranking and no cutoff, so it is the most sensitive of the three and the most prone to calling pathways in a dataset where no single CpG reaches epigenome-wide significance. Its p-values also come from random permutations: the chunk above fixes the seed so the table is the same on every render, but without the seed, two otherwise identical runs called eleven and nine pathways significant. A result that changes with the random seed is not one to write up on its own; it would need to be confirmed with a different method or in another cohort.

Code 
# written by the `methylgsa` chunk above
# KEGG ids are zero-padded ("05223"), so read them as text
rra <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
# NES is only present when the file came from a GSEA run, so take the columns
# that are there instead of failing the render on a missing one
rra_cols <- intersect(c("KEGG", "Pathway", "Size", "NES", "pvalue", "padj"), names(rra))
knitr::kable(rra[, ..rra_cols],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "The five top-ranked methylRRA-GSEA KEGG pathways. All five pass FDR < 0.05 (eight pathways do in total) on a dataset with no epigenome-wide signal, which is the sensitivity/specificity trade-off of a cutoff-free rank test made concrete.")
The five top-ranked methylRRA-GSEA KEGG pathways. All five pass FDR < 0.05 (eight pathways do in total) on a dataset with no epigenome-wide signal, which is the sensitivity/specificity trade-off of a cutoff-free rank test made concrete.
KEGG Pathway Size NES pvalue padj

ImportantThe tool is a modeling choice, not a lookup

Report the method and its settings, not just “KEGG enrichment.” A reviewer who reruns your CpGs through a different tool will get a different list, and that is expected — gometh, methylglm, and methylRRA encode different assumptions about how probe density biases the test. Pick one a priori (we default to gometh for its conservative, well-validated behavior), and if you report a second for sensitivity, say so and show both. Never run all three and present the one with the prettiest pathway.

KnowYourCG (KYCG): CpG-centric enrichment on regulatory elements

gometh asks a gene-set question — it collapses your CpGs to genes and tests GO/KEGG. But methylation acts through regulatory elements — CpG islands, transcription-factor binding sites, chromatin states, histone marks — and collapsing to genes throws that resolution away. KnowYourCG (KYCG), part of Zhou’s sesame/knowYourCG ecosystem (Goldberg et al. 2025), keeps the CpG as the unit of analysis and tests your hit set directly against curated databases of these elements. It is the CpG-centric complement to gometh, not a replacement, and it comes from the same lab as the annotation we used in Part 1.

The knowledgebases are keyed by probe ID, so there are no coordinates to line up, but they were not all built on the same genome. The CpG-island knowledgebase is derived from the hg38 manifest’s CGIposition column (the same source as Part 1’s island context), while the chromatin-state knowledgebase comes from Roadmap chromHMM states annotated on hg19. The transcription-factor and histone-mark knowledgebases are hg38: they were built by intersecting ChIP-seq peaks from the Cistrome Data Browser with the array’s CpG coordinates (Goldberg et al. 2025), and Cistrome maps all human data to hg38 (Zheng et al. 2019).

Code 
library(knowYourCG)
library(sesameData)

# Download the EPIC knowledgebases into the ExperimentHub cache. testEnrichment()
# stops with 'either not found or needs to be cached' until this has run once;
# after that it is a no-op.
kycgDataCache()
tt      <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
all.cpg <- tt$probe                              # universe = every CpG you tested
sig.cpg <- tt[order(bacon.p)][1:1000]$probe   # your query set

# What CpG-feature databases are available for this platform?
# ALWAYS list first: the catalog names carry datestamps and they change
# between releases. A wrong name fails at load time, not at test time.
listDBGroups("EPIC")           # EPIC knowledgebases: CGI, TFBS, chromHMM, HM, ...
Code 
# Cache the databases you want from ExperimentHub, then test.
dbs <- c("KYCG.EPIC.CGI.20210713",               # CpG-island relation
         "KYCG.EPIC.chromHMM.20211020",          # chromatin states
         "KYCG.EPIC.TFBSconsensus.20211013",     # TF binding sites
         "KYCG.EPIC.HMconsensus.20211013")       # histone marks
res <- testEnrichment(query = sig.cpg, databases = dbs,
                      universe = all.cpg, platform = "EPIC")
res <- res[order(res$FDR), ]

# All 863 tested features, one row each: the deposited result table, and the
# input to every KYCG number quoted below.
data.table::fwrite(res, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_results.csv")

testEnrichment runs a Fisher test of your query CpGs against each database, using your tested set as the universe (the same universe discipline that matters for gometh). The databases are versioned knowledgebases pulled from ExperimentHub, so the run is reproducible.

The universe is all 756,251 tested CpGs and the query is the same top 1,000 used for gometh, tested against 863 features across the four knowledgebases. That number matters for the interpretation below — the four databases are wildly different sizes.

knowYourCG applies the Benjamini–Hochberg correction within each knowledgebase, not across all 863 features at once. That is a choice with consequences: a feature in the five-row CpG-island knowledgebase is corrected against four others, while a transcription-factor feature is corrected against 782. Earlier releases of knowYourCG corrected across all 863; with that correction the same p-values give 2 significant features rather than 5, and the difference is the H1.4, H3K9me2 and 8_ZNF/Rpts results discussed below. Check which correction your version applies before you report a count.

On our teaching subset KYCG returns 5 features at FDR < 0.05 where gometh returned nothing. The two results are not directly comparable. They ask different questions: gometh collapses CpGs to genes and tests pathways, while KYCG keeps the CpG as the unit and tests which regulatory elements the CpGs fall in. Their annotations also differ: gometh’s gene assignments here come from Zhou’s hg38 GENCODE v41 manifest, whereas KYCG’s features come from Zhou’s knowledgebases, which are hg38 except for the hg19 chromatin states. The count of 5 also needs care, because KYCG’s feature sets are large and overlap heavily; the callout below works through what those 5 features do and do not show.

Code 
top12 <- head(as.data.table(res)[order(FDR, p.value)], 12)
top12[, kb := sub("^KYCG[.]EPIC[.]", "", sub("[.][0-9]+$", "", group))]
top12[, dbname := factor(dbname, levels = rev(dbname))]
ggplot(top12, aes(x = estimate, y = dbname, fill = kb)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(CGI = "#8C3A4A", chromHMM = "#B8883E",
                               HMconsensus = "#5B7F95", TFBSconsensus = "#1A6B75")) +
  labs(x = "log2 odds ratio", y = NULL, fill = "knowledgebase")
Code 
# This chunk executes: it reads the result table the chunk above wrote and
# derives the three summaries the rest of this section discusses, so none of
# those numbers can drift away from the run that produced them.
k <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_kycg_results.csv")
# testEnrichment names the knowledgebase in `group` and the feature in `dbname`,
# which reads backwards; rename once here
setnames(k, c("group", "dbname"), c("db", "feature"))
# drop the "KYCG.EPIC." prefix and the release datestamp: "CGI", "chromHMM", ...
k[, kb := sub("^KYCG\\.EPIC\\.", "", sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", db))]

# per-knowledgebase: how much was tested, how much survived, and the leader
ksum <- k[, .(
  `Features tested` = .N,
  `Nominal p<0.05`  = sum(p.value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  `FDR<0.05`        = sum(FDR < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  `Top feature`     = feature[which.min(FDR)],
  `Top log2(OR)`    = round(estimate[which.min(FDR)], 2),
  `Top FDR`         = signif(min(FDR, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
), by = .(Knowledgebase = kb)][order(-`FDR<0.05`)]
fwrite(ksum, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_db_summary.csv")

# every feature that clears FDR < 0.05, best first
ktop <- k[FDR < 0.05][order(FDR, p.value),
  .(Knowledgebase = kb, Feature = feature,
    `log2(OR)` = round(estimate, 2), `Query CpGs` = overlap,
    `DB size` = nD, p = signif(p.value, 3), FDR = signif(FDR, 3))]
fwrite(ktop, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_top.csv")

# the CGI knowledgebase in full — all five rows, significant or not, because the
# section below reads it as a negative result and needs the near-misses visible
kcgi <- k[kb == "CGI"][order(FDR),
  .(Feature = feature, `log2(OR)` = round(estimate, 2),
    `Query CpGs` = overlap, `DB size` = nD,
    p = signif(p.value, 3), FDR = signif(FDR, 3))]
fwrite(kcgi, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_cgi.csv")
Code

  caption = "KYCG results per knowledgebase. The four databases differ in size by two orders of magnitude, and the largest one contributes only one of the significant hits.")

Read that table before reading the hits. Three things fall out of it:

  • The 5 hits are not spread evenly — 1 of 5 comes from TFBSconsensus, which contributes 783 of the 863 features tested. Three come from histone marks, one from chromatin state, and none from CpG-island relation.
  • 8_ZNF/Rpts (ZNF genes and repeats) is the single chromatin-state hit (log₂OR = 1.96, FDR = 0.039), from only 7 of the 1,000 query CpGs; 1_TssA (active TSS) is not significant (log₂OR = 0.27, FDR = 0.077), consistent with the absence of a promoter lean in Figure 1.
  • The CpG-island knowledgebase has no hit. Islands are barely enriched (log₂OR = 0.06, nominal p = 0.30, FDR = 0.50) when corrected against the other four island categories. The visual island lean in Figure 2 (19.9% vs 19.2%) is therefore not supported by the formal test.
